rules.rule:
These are QNSC's own review rules. They sit ON TOP of the built-in language rules, which
already cover hardcoding, magic values, dead code, null handling and the usual correctness
and security questions — do not repeat those here. Everything below is a convention a
general-purpose reviewer cannot infer from the code alone, and each one is written because it
was got wrong in this organisation at least once.

## A comment says why, not what

Comments in this codebase explain the reason a thing is the way it is — the constraint, the
alternative that failed, the incident. A comment restating the code adds a line to maintain
and nothing else.

- Flag a comment that paraphrases the statement below it.
- Flag a non-obvious decision with no comment: an unusual constant, a workaround, a
  deliberate omission, an ordering that matters.
- Do NOT ask for comments on self-evident code.

## A guard that cannot fail is worse than no guard

A check which passes regardless of input gives false confidence and is harder to notice than
a missing check. Real examples from this organisation: a `git grep -E '\b...'` that silently
matched nothing because POSIX ERE has no `\b`, so a search for old references reported clean;
a coverage threshold that the runner ignored; tests that passed because a local `.env`
supplied the value they were asserting was absent.

- Flag a new test or CI step that would still pass if the thing it protects were removed.
- Flag an assertion whose expected value is derived from the same code under test.
- For a guard against a value being present, require that something sets that value — a
  canary — or the guard proves nothing.

## Configuration that is consumed must be declared

Where a value is read, it must also be declared in whatever mechanism makes it reachable:
env schema, install prompts, manifest, Terraform variable, workflow input. A value read but
not declared appears to work in development, where the developer's own environment supplies
it, and is absent for everyone else.

- Flag a new environment variable read in code that is not added to the declaring schema.
- Flag a new required input that has no default and no documentation.

## Do not hardcode a host, endpoint or identifier

Hosts belong in configuration with a documented default. Nineteen bundled servers once
shipped pointing at hostnames that had never had DNS records, and nothing failed until
someone called them.

- Flag a literal URL, hostname, IP, account id, ARN or tenant id outside configuration.
- Flag a new external endpoint with no timeout and no error path.

## Documentation must not claim something untrue

A README that describes an intention rather than the state of the repository is a defect, not
a style problem. This organisation shipped seven documents saying no binaries were published
while nine releases existed, and a generated file that claimed to be generated and was not.

- Flag a doc change that contradicts the code in the same pull request.
- Flag a file that says it is generated when nothing generates it.
- Flag a count, version or tool list stated as fact where the source of truth disagrees.

## Secrets

- Nothing secret may be logged, interpolated into an error, or written to a build artifact.
- Obfuscation is not protection. A value recoverable from something you ship is public.
- Flag a credential that would end up in a compiled binary, image layer or committed file.

## Pull request hygiene

- The title must be Conventional Commits: the changelog and the next version are derived from
  it, so a malformed title is a release defect rather than a style nit.
- Avoid nested parentheses in a commit body; the release tool fails to parse them and
  silently produces no release.
- Flag a change that mixes an unrelated file into a focused pull request.
